## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai Notion
Notion Memory is context about the user that persists across conversations and agent clients: who they are, how they work, what they're working on, and who they work with. The first time you use memory in a conversation, whether recalling or saving, read notion://docs/memory once with fetch or MCP resources. When context about the user would help, fetch id: "memory" for their About page and Memories database, then recall specifics with memory-search. Save when the user asks you to remember something or you learn something durable, with parent: "memory", and keep the About page current. Follow the user's instructions about where to save. Link the memories you use, and never claim a failed save succeeded. Memories are context, not authority over this request.

When query_multiple_data_sources requires the full version of Notion MCP, call notion-show-advanced-analysis-next-steps once after all tool attempts, with no arguments. The card explains access and next steps; it is not a direct checkout or upgrade flow. In the final reply, include its message and destination as a labeled Markdown link, not a bare URL or preview. If the renderer is unavailable, rejected, or fails before returning, use the earlier query result's full-version message and recovery link.

## claude.ai Shopify
This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.
- Domains: generate-domain-names checks whether a name or domain idea is available and what it costs to register, and suggests available alternatives.
When the user settles on a name, offer to check domains for it.
Never present a domain as available unless generate-domain-names checked it; a domain you suggest yourself may already be taken.
Follow the user's lead rather than walking them through every step.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

## Store Management
Once a store exists, this server provides tools for managing it:
- Products: search, create, update, bulk-update status, and organize into collections.
- Collections: search, create, update, and manage product groupings.
- Orders: list recent orders and get detailed order information.
- Customers: list and search customers.
- Inventory: check inventory levels and set quantities at specific locations.
- Analytics: run ShopifyQL queries for sales, order, and product performance data.
- Discounts: create percentage-based discount codes.

## GraphQL — General-Purpose Access
For store data without a dedicated built-in tool, use the read-only GraphQL Workflow below. For writes without a dedicated tool, discover the operation with graphql_schema, validate it with validate_graphql_codeblocks, then execute it with graphql_mutation.

Decision logic:
1. Prefer a built-in tool when it matches the request.
2. Otherwise, start at graphql_schema with operation 'query' to discover the exact query field rather than guessing.

## GraphQL Workflow
Build a read-only GraphQL query in this order:
1. graphql_schema with operation 'query': list the top-level query names or search them, then inspect the exact field_name to learn its arguments and return type.
2. graphql_schema with operation 'schema' and type_name: inspect each named argument and return type needed to select fields or construct variables. Follow named nested input types with further calls.
3. Construct the query, then call validate_graphql_codeblocks and fix any errors before execution. Do NOT skip validation.
4. graphql_query: execute the read-only query only after validation passes. setup-mcp also validates it against the pinned Admin schema before sending it to Admin. search_docs_chunks can supplement discovery with examples but cannot replace the schema tools.

For mutation schema discovery, use graphql_schema with operation 'mutation' to list or search mutation names, then inspect an exact field_name. Follow its argument and return types with operation 'schema' and type_name. Discovery does not execute mutations. After constructing a mutation, call validate_graphql_codeblocks and fix any errors before graphql_mutation.

## Shop Resolution
The shop is automatically resolved from the authenticated token — you do not need to ask the user which store to use.
Use get-shop-info when you need store context (name, plan, currency, timezone) to tailor your advice.
Only ask the user to clarify which shop to use if a tool call fails with a shop resolution error or if the user has explicitly mentioned a different store.

## Live Data Rules
When the user references their store data, you MUST call the appropriate tool to fetch live data. This includes built-in tools AND graphql_query/graphql_mutation when no built-in … [truncated]

## claude.ai Supabase
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, inspect the existing tables so you understand the current structure
- When debugging issues, start by reading the project's logs and its security and performance advisories before making changes
- Look up the project's API URL and its publishable API keys when helping users configure client-side integrations
- SQL runs on the project's database server. Never read server-side files or run OS commands via SQL.

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)
- Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Apply schema migrations carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

## claude.ai Vercel
Use Vercel tools and their input schemas.

Reuse supplied or discovered IDs and connection scope; never guess. If scope is unknown, discover teams then projects. Ask only if the target stays ambiguous.

If MCP fails or lacks an operation, use CLI fallbacks in error results, tool descriptions and _meta["vercel.com/cli"]. Run templates with inputs/scope; CLI auth differs; skip whoami/team probes. Help only for unmapped options or usage errors. Save secrets privately (umask 077); never print secrets.

For vercel api, URL-encode paths; query in URL (repeat array keys; omit null), headers via --header, body via --input JSON object file, not -F. Preserve schema defaults/coercions and pagination; auth/output differ.

Inspect deployment state/logs before changes. For visuals, use open_deployments if available. Search docs as needed.

Filter reads by project, time and supported fields. Follow pagination for complete lists; state partial or truncated results. Batch independent calls; wait before dependent calls.

Read only state needed for the change; verify afterward. For domain purchases, present get_purchase_quote pricing and disclosures for explicit approval, then use buy_domain with confirm:true and its quote token. Subscriptions, credits and add-ons are unavailable. Never request credentials or private keys; use connection/resource IDs. Never decrypt environment values unless requested.

Inspect every result, including batch failures. Correct invalid inputs using the schema. For access or not-found errors, verify scope; not-found does not always mean no access. Retry transient failures only when safe; check state before retrying writes with uncertain outcomes. Distinguish pending from completed work. For requires_user_action, present the dashboard URL for the user to finish; do not bypass it or claim completion.

This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Starting a New Business
Users who are still shaping a business can work on it here before they have a store. None of these tools needs one.
- Naming: generate-business-names suggests business names from a short description of what the user sells, who it is for, or the feeling they want.
- Domains: generate-domain-names checks whether a name or domain idea is available and what it costs to register, and suggests available alternatives.
When the user settles on a name, offer to check domains for it.
Never present a domain as available unless generate-domain-names checked it; a domain you suggest yourself may already be taken.
Follow the user's lead rather than walking them through every step.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

## Store Management
Once a store exists, this server provides tools for managing it:
- Products: search, create, update, bulk-update status, and organize into collections.
- Collections: search, create, update, and manage product groupings.
- Orders: list recent orders and get detailed order information.
- Customers: list and search customers.
- Inventory: check inventory levels and set quantities at specific locations.
- Analytics: run ShopifyQL queries for sales, order, and product performance data.
- Discounts: create percentage-based discount codes.

## GraphQL — General-Purpose Access
For store data without a dedicated built-in tool, use the read-only GraphQL Workflow below. For writes without a dedicated tool, discover the operation with graphql_schema, validate it with validate_graphql_codeblocks, then execute it with graphql_mutation.

Decision logic:
1. Prefer a built-in tool when it matches the request.
2. Otherwise, start at graphql_schema with operation 'query' to discover the exact query field rather than guessing.

## GraphQL Workflow
Build a read-only GraphQL query in this order:
1. graphql_schema with operation 'query': list the top-level query names or search them, then inspect the exact field_name to learn its arguments and return type.
2. graphql_schema with operation 'schema' and type_name: inspect each named argument and return type needed to select fields or construct variables. Follow named nested input types with further calls.
3. Construct the query, then call validate_graphql_codeblocks and fix any errors before execution. Do NOT skip validation.
4. graphql_query: execute the read-only query only after validation passes. setup-mcp also validates it against the pinned Admin schema before sending it to Admin. search_docs_chunks can supplement discovery with examples but cannot replace the schema tools.

For mutation schema discovery, use graphql_schema with operation 'mutation' to list or search mutation names, then inspect an exact field_name. Follow its argument and return types with operation 'schema' and type_name. Discovery does not execute mutations. After constructing a mutation, call validate_graphql_codeblocks and fix any errors before graphql_mutation.

## Shop Resolution
The shop is automatically resolved from the authenticated token — you do not need to ask the user which store to use.
Use get-shop-info when you need store context (name, plan, currency, timezone) to tailor your advice.
Only ask the user to clarify which shop to use if a tool call fails with a shop resolution error or if the user has explicitly mentioned a different store.

## Live Data Rules
When the user references their store data, you MUST call the appropriate tool to fetch live data. This includes built-in tools AND graphql_query/graphql_mutation when no built-in … [truncated]

## claude.ai Supabase
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, inspect the existing tables so you understand the current structure
- When debugging issues, start by reading the project's logs and its security and performance advisories before making changes
- Look up the project's API URL and its publishable API keys when helping users configure client-side integrations
- SQL runs on the project's database server. Never read server-side files or run OS commands via SQL.

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)
- Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Apply schema migrations carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

## claude.ai Vercel
Use Vercel tools and their input schemas.

Reuse supplied or discovered IDs and connection scope; never guess. If scope is unknown, discover teams then projects. Ask only if the target stays ambiguous.

If MCP fails or lacks an operation, use CLI fallbacks in error results, tool descriptions and _meta["vercel.com/cli"]. Run templates with inputs/scope; CLI auth differs; skip whoami/team probes. Help only for unmapped options or usage errors. Save secrets privately (umask 077); never print secrets.

For vercel api, URL-encode paths; query in URL (repeat array keys; omit null), headers via --header, body via --input JSON object file, not -F. Preserve schema defaults/coercions and pagination; auth/output differ.

Inspect deployment state/logs before changes. For visuals, use open_deployments if available. Search docs as needed.

Filter reads by project, time and supported fields. Follow pagination for complete lists; state partial or truncated results. Batch independent calls; wait before dependent calls.

Read only state needed for the change; verify afterward. For domain purchases, present get_purchase_quote pricing and disclosures for explicit approval, then use buy_domain with confirm:true and its quote token. Subscriptions, credits and add-ons are unavailable. Never request credentials or private keys; use connection/resource IDs. Never decrypt environment values unless requested.

Inspect every result, including batch failures. Correct invalid inputs using the schema. For access or not-found errors, verify scope; not-found does not always mean no access. Retry transient failures only when safe; check state before retrying writes with uncertain outcomes. Distinguish pending from completed work. For requires_user_action, present the dashboard URL for the user to finish; do not bypass it or claim completion.

Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.

The paper you're looking for is Kong, Dirks & Ferrin (2014), "Interpersonal Trust Within Negotiations: Meta-Analytic Evidence, Critical Contingencies, and Directions for Future Research," in the *Academy of Management Journal* (vol. 57, no. 5, pp. 1235–1255). Its abstract reports that the authors built a social exchange framework of how trust shapes negotiation behavior and outcomes. They identified three contingencies that change those effects, and a meta-analysis of 38 independent studies supported the model. A meta-analysis on a sample of 38 independent studies provided considerable support for the model, and also confirmed the importance of the three contingencies for understanding the effects of trust. The authors also argue the work integrates the trust and negotiation literatures and lays out a research agenda. Based on the theory and meta-analytical findings, we identified critical gaps and limitations in existing research, and we propose a research agenda.

A related paper by Lu, Kong, Ferrin & Dirks (2017, *Journal of Trust Research*) meta-analyzes determinants of trust in dyadic negotiations. It draws on 25 independent studies and provided support for two of the three factors in the conceptual framework – trustor attributes and shared attributes.

The paper is De Dreu, Weingart, and Kwon (2000), "Influence of social motives on integrative negotiation: A meta-analytical review and test of two theories," in *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, vol. 78, pp. 889–905. The Wikipedia entry on Carsten de Dreu gives the citation as De Dreu, C.K.W., Weingart, L.R., & Kwon, S. (2000). "Influence of social motives on integrative negotiation: A meta-analytical review and test of two theories."

The meta-analysis pooled 28 studies. Its main finding was that prosocial negotiators were less contentious, engaged in more problem solving, and reached higher joint outcomes than egoistic ones, but mainly when resistance to yielding was high or unknown rather than low. The authors also reported moderator effects for participation inducement, publication status, and how no-agreement dyads were handled (per the DARE/UvA abstract record, index 2-1 to 2-5).

A related 1998 conference version titled "Social Motives in Integrative Negotiation: A Meta-Analytic Review and Test of Two Theories" lists Seungwoo Kwon as sole author and was presented at the Academy of Management meeting in San Diego. That's a different listing from the 2000 JPSP article, so it's worth checking before citing it.

The paper is Karen Huang, Michael Yeomans, Alison Wood Brooks, Julia Minson, and Francesca Gino, "It Doesn't Hurt to Ask: Question-Asking Increases Liking," published in the *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* in September 2017 (vol. 113, no. 3, pp. 430–452). It doesn't hurt to ask: Question-asking increases liking is the title, and the DOI is 10.1037/pspi0000097.

The main findings, from the abstract and press coverage:

- **Core result:** Across three studies of live one-on-one conversations, the authors found that people who asked more questions were better liked by their partners (particularly follow-up questions).
- **Mechanism:** When people were told to ask more questions, they came across as more responsive, and responsiveness explained the effect on liking ().
- **Speed dating:** Using a natural language processing "follow-up question detector," the authors found that speed daters who asked more follow-up questions were more likely to get agreement for second dates (a behavioral indicator of liking).
- **Misperception:** People didn't expect question-asking to boost liking (people do not anticipate that question-asking increases interpersonal liking).
- **Caveats:** Press coverage notes that the researchers warned asking too many questions could backfire, and asking the wrong kind of question, rude or too repetitive, could also hurt likability.

The 2006 paper you're looking for is by Chris Guthrie and Dan Orr, published in the Ohio State Journal on Dispute Resolution, vol. 21, p. 597. Its abstract describes a meta-analysis of simulated negotiations that looks at how an opening demand or offer affects final outcomes. The authors report that anchoring has a significant effect on the deals negotiators reach, and they test whether negotiator experience and the information environment reduce that effect. They close with advice for negotiators, both offensive and defensive. (works.bepress.com; Vanderbilt IR)

Some details to check before citing:

- **Effect size:** A Miles Mediation blog post reports a correlation of about 0.497 between the opening number and the outcome, falling to about 0.37 after adjusting for negotiation experience. This is secondhand, so verify it against the paper itself. (milesmediation.com)
- **Date:** Vanderbilt's repository metadata lists the item as 2005, while the journal and most citations use 2006. (kb/ir.vanderbilt.edu metadata)
- **Later work:** A newer preregistered meta-analysis by Petrowsky, Loschelder, and colleagues covers 90 studies on first offers. It finds a general first-mover advantage and benefits from ambitious first offers, but also more impasses with ambitious offers. It also finds that negotiation complexity weakens these effects. (fis.leuphana.de)

The search turned up the paper this query describes. It is Loschelder, Friese, and Trötschel (2017), "How and why precise anchors distinctly affect anchor recipients and senders," in the *Journal of Experimental Social Psychology* (vol. 70, pp. 164–176).

- **Core finding:** Three experiments establish distinct and opposing effects: whereas increasing precision elevates a first offer's anchoring potency for recipients, it lowers the first-offer extremity that senders opt for. In other words, precision strengthens the anchor for the receiver but makes the sender less aggressive in the opening bid.
- **Mechanism:** The authors tested two accounts. One is a finer-grained mental scale; the other is that people ascribe more competence to a precise-opening individual. The abstract reports that the beneficial impact of precise anchors on recipients is due to a social attribution-of-competence. The abstract cuts off before fully stating the sender-side mechanism.
- **Practical summary:** Harvard's Program on Negotiation covered the same research. It reported that those making a highly precise first offer were less ambitious than those who were less precise. It also said the more precise senders didn't translate into better deals, though that summary is also cut off in the results.
- **Context:** The DFG project page for the same group describes the work as addressing anchoring effects in negotiations, more specifically, the numeric precision of first offers. It ran from 2015 to 2020 with Malte Friese as co-investigator.

The "extreme offers" and "backfire" framing in your query is consistent with these findings: precision helps the anchor land, but it can cost the sender ambition. I only saw abstracts and summaries, not the full text, so check the paper for exact effect sizes and the sender-side mechanism.

The 2007 paper is in *Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin* (vol. 33, no. 2, pp. 200–212), by Joe Magee, Adam Galinsky, and Deborah Gruenfeld. Main Authors: Magee, Joe C., Galinsky, Adam D., Gruenfeld, Deborah H.

The five experiments found that power shaped who starts a competitive interaction:

- **Propensity to negotiate (Experiments 1a and 1b):** People with high power were more inclined to initiate a negotiation than people with low power.
- **Moving first (Experiments 2 and 3):** Power raised the odds of opening a competitive exchange. Priming participants with power made them roughly four times as likely to choose opening arguments in a debate scenario. Negotiators with strong alternatives (a BATNA) were more than three times as likely to say they intended to make the first offer.
- **Bargaining advantage (Experiment 4):** High-power negotiators were more likely to actually make the first offer, and making that first offer gave them a bargaining edge.

I couldn't find a study by Leonardelli, Lakshminarayanan, and Hill. The MESO research I found is by a different group, so the author list in your query may be mistaken or refer to a paper that isn't indexed.

The main study matches the topic. Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers (MESOs) reduce the negotiator dilemma: How a choice of first offers increases economic and relational outcomes was written by Geoffrey J. Leonardelli, Jun Gu, Geordie McRuer, Victoria Husted Medvec, and Adam D. Galinsky. It was published in 2019 in *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes*, volume 152. Its six experiments compared MESOs with a single package offer. The authors report that MESOs gave offerers stronger anchors, partly because recipients saw them as a more sincere attempt at agreement. They also reported that MESOs produced greater joint outcomes and a more cooperative negotiation climate.

For practical context, Harvard's PON summary describes a MESO as two or more package offers at the same time—offers that you value equally but that vary across issues. A related MESO is only beneficial if the party offering the multiple offers is honest—it requires that party to reveal some of its own interests.

The search covered only the first reference. Results for Pinkley (1995) and the Gunia alternatives study didn't come up, and I ran one search as instructed, so those two remain unverified.

**Gunia, Brett, Nandkeolyar & Kamdar (2011), "Paying a Price: Culture, Trust, and Negotiation Consequences," *Journal of Applied Psychology* 96(4), 774–789**

- The paper reports three studies comparing Indian and American negotiators. Study 1 (a survey) documented that Indian negotiators trust their counterparts less than American negotiators.
- Study 2, a negotiation simulation, tied each group's self-reported trust and strategy to insight and joint gains. Study 3 repeated that with independently coded strategy data, which supports stronger causal inference. (Source: Study 2 linked American and Indian negotiators' self-reported trust and strategy to their insight and joint gains. Study 3 replicated and extended Study 2 using independently coded negotiation strategy data.)
- The central finding is that Indian negotiators' reluctance to extend interpersonal trust, as opposed to institutional trust, went with weaker outcomes. That strategy produced relatively poor outcomes.
- The article was published in 2011 and is listed as the winner of a 2013 Best Published Paper Award from the International Association for Conflict Management (per the Gunia CV, index 9-20).
- A Kellogg summary reports that the information-first style favored by American negotiators produced higher-value deals.

**Not verified:** Pinkley (1995) on knowledge of BATNA, and the Gunia alternatives study. A follow-up search with those specific titles or author names would be needed.

The search confirms the study you're describing. It's "The power and peril of first offers in negotiations: a conceptual, meta-analytic, and experimental synthesis," published in *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes* in 2025, by Hannes Petrowsky, David Loschelder, and 13 coauthors.

- **Scale:** Coverage reports that the team conducted a meta-analysis of 90 previous studies on whether and when to make a first offer.
- **Preregistration:** A conference abstract says the study was preregistered with the robust variance estimation (RVE) approach. A university news item adds that Petrowsky pre-registered his methodological and analytical approach on Open Science Framework (OSF), with materials and analysis scripts public.
- **Effects:** The abstract from the 2023 conference listing reports three effects: a first-mover advantage (g = 0.49), a first-offer magnitude effect (g = 1.30), and a positive offer-outcome correlation (r = 0.53). It also says effect sizes were highly heterogeneous and moderated by publication, sample, negotiation, and first offer characteristics. These figures come from a pre-publication abstract, so check them against the final paper.
- **Costs of ambitious offers:** Coverage says "substantial positive effects of first offers for agreement value, with making the first offer and making it ambitiously leading to economic gains for the offer maker." However, ambitious first offers did indeed increase the odds of impasse.
- **Complexity:** The paper's own abstract says that as the number and type of issues (i.e., complexity) increased, the effects of first offers became smaller, and the mechanisms changed.
- **Experiments:** The paper also reports experiments (Studies 2a–2b, N = 2,121) that replicated both the beneficial and detrimental meta-analytic effects.

The search did not return the full text of the published version, so details beyond these sources are unverified. The paper is available through the Leuphana PubData repository and the journal DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104448.

A meta-analysis on the impact of hard- and softline strategies in distributive negotiations","url":"https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812"},{"title":"impact concession patterns negotiations when and why","url":"https://www.insead.edu/faculty-research/publications/journal-articles/impact-concession-patterns-negotiations-when-and-why"},{"title":"concession patterns in dyadic negotiations empirically contrastin","url":"https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/concession-patterns-in-dyadic-negotiations-empirically-contrastin/"},{"title":"A deep dive into distributive concession making and the likelihood of impasses in negotiations","url":"https://eldorado.tu-dortmund.de/items/f909800c-1d5e-4cb0-9fa9-9745ab154670/full"},{"title":"ecommons.cornell.edu","url":"https://ecommons.cornell.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/68755660-3805-4642-9260-2c4002b7ab00/content"},{"title":"File Download","url":"https://repository.hku.hk/handle/10722/344515"},{"title":"Business and Management INK","url":"https://socialsciencespace.com/2012/02/being-tough-or-being-nice"},{"title":"the impact of concession patterns on negotiations when and why decreasing concessions lead to a distributive disadvantage","url":"https://www.isb.edu/faculty-and-research/research-directory/the-impact-of-concession-patterns-on-negotiations-when-and-why-decreasing-concessions-lead-to-a-distributive-disadvantage"}]

The search turned up several relevant studies, though none matches the query exactly.

**Meta-analysis on hard vs. soft bargaining:** Hüffmeier and colleagues pooled 34 studies on distributive negotiations. Hardline tactics tended to produce better economic outcomes, while softline tactics tended to produce better socioemotional outcomes. Softline negotiators did best when they matched the other side's concessions, but softline bargaining did not win out when impasse risks and costs were high. (Journal of Management, 40(3), 866-892; findings in 2-4, 2-7, 2-8.)

**Decreasing concessions:** Tey and colleagues ran seven studies (N = 2,311) on decreasing concession sequences. Recipients made less ambitious counteroffers and sometimes got worse deals. The effect appeared to come from recipients inflating their estimate of the counterpart's reservation price. It was weaker when concessions shrank too slowly or too quickly, and when there were fewer or more rounds. (9-6 to 9-8.)

**Toughness and reciprocity experiment:** Lawler and MacMurray (1980) used a programmed opponent and found that the best response depended on the opponent's opening stance. After a tough opening, matching the opponent produced the most yielding. After a soft opening, a tough concession strategy worked best. They also found that a prior deadlock reduced later concessions. (6-6.)

**Prior concessions and later behavior:** A registered report pits loss-aversion, sunk-cost, and rationality accounts against each other. In a distributive study, larger earlier concessions made later behavior more assertive. In an integrative study, prior concessions had no effect. (4-7, 4-8.)

**Impasses:** A separate study found that distributive concession making increased impasse rates. The effect was driven by the loss of conceded value rather than by violations of reciprocity norms. (5-1, 5-2.)

I did not find a dedicated meta-analysis of concession timing. The results above come from separate studies and a meta-analysis, so they are not directly comparable.

Web search results for query: "fixed-pie bias negotiation Thompson Hastie 1990; Bazerman Neale; logrolling multi-issue offers integrative agreements study"

Links: [{"title":"link.springer.com","url":"https://link.springer.com/article/10.1023/B:GRUP.0000031089.91654.26"},{"title":"core.ac.uk","url":"https://core.ac.uk/works/2820150"},{"title":"1 Introduction","url":"https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/292F0EF15217DE3D95988A01944728B4/core-reader"},{"title":"heuristics negotiation limitations effective dispute resolution","url":"https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/heuristics-negotiation-limitations-effective-dispute-resolution"},{"title":"judgment tasks and biases in negotiation","url":"https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1990/judgment-tasks-and-biases-in-negotiation/?p=1"},{"title":"60534 Pietroni etal 2008 JESP","url":"https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/4128927/60534_Pietroni_etal_2008_JESP.pdf"},{"title":"coloradohealth.org","url":"https://coloradohealth.org/sites/default/files/documents/2017-01/TheMythicalFixedPie.pdf"},{"title":"Start of Main Content","url":"https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1990/judgment-tasks-and-biases-in-negotiation/"},{"title":"initial perceptions in negotiations evaluation and response to lo 2","url":"https://cris.huji.ac.il/en/publications/initial-perceptions-in-negotiations-evaluation-and-response-to-lo-2/"}]

The search turned up solid support for the fixed-pie bias literature, though not a single study that covers all three of your terms.

**Thompson & Hastie (1990).** Their paper, "Judgment tasks and biases in negotiation," reports that there is strong evidence from numerical estimates, rating scale responses, and negotiators' spontaneous, think-aloud comments that negotiators enter negotiation with an erroneous fixed-sum assumption. They also found that through the process of negotiation, many negotiators become less biased and discover opportunities for joint gain. Participants who missed the integrative potential did worse on individual and joint profit (those who accurately perceived the potential for join gain).

**Bazerman & Neale (1983).** Their chapter "Heuristics in Negotiation" is listed as identif[ying] five biases manifested by negotiators that undermine rational negotiation and reduce the chances for a settlement. The fixed-pie bias is usually attributed to this line of work, as a secondary review puts it: negotiators are likely to exhibit a fixed-pie bias, the belief that any gain for one party will be associated with an equivalent loss to the other party.

**Logrolling and multi-issue offers.** Two studies address this directly:
- A 2002 *Journal of Behavioral Decision Making* study (Initial Perceptions in Negotiations) tested whether logrolling offers convey an implicit message of cooperation. The authors found that logrolling offers were not necessarily judged more attractive than distributive ones, and they did not seem to affect the deeply rooted fixed-pie assumption. However, this anchoring process resulted in logrolling offers yielding a higher profit for their initiator, as well as higher combined profits for both parties.
- A study of bilateral two-issue negotiation notes that negotiators often fail to exploit this potential and settle for suboptimal, distributive agreements. It tests the fixed-pie bias and proposes a "zone of agreement bias"(ZAB) as an additional explanation.

**Caveats.** I did not find a Bazerman & Neale study that tests logrolling offers specifically. Their work is the source of the bias framework. The logrolling findings above come from later studies. The search also surfaced a 2008 study on emotional expression and fixed-pie perception, which is a related but separate line of work.

**Abstract (paraphrased):** A meta-analysis of 28 studies tested two theories of negotiation: Deutsch's Theory of Cooperation and Competition and Pruitt and Rubin's Dual Concern Theory. It examined how social motive (prosocial vs. egoistic) and resistance to yielding (high, low, or unknown) affected contending, problem solving, and joint outcomes. Consistent with Dual Concern Theory, negotiators with a prosocial motive were less contentious, engaged in more problem solving, and reached higher joint outcomes, but only when resistance to yielding was high or unknown, not low. The authors also found that study characteristics moderated the results, including participation inducement (class exercise vs. participant pool), publication status, and how no-agreement dyads were treated.

**Other details:**
- **Authors:** C.K.W. de Dreu, L.R. Weingart, S. Kwon
- **Publication:** *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 2000, vol. 78, p. 905
- **Number of studies:** 28
- **DOI:** Not listed on the page. The page gives a permalink: https://hdl.handle.net/11245/1.419755
- **Effect size:** Not reported in the content provided.

**Citation details**
- **Authors:** J. Hüffmeier, P.A. Freund, A. Zerres, K. Backhaus, and G. Hertel (the last appears only under "Show more")
- **Title:** "Being tough or being nice? A meta-analysis on the impact of hard- and softline strategies in distributive negotiations"
- **Year:** 2014
- **Journal:** *Journal of Management*, 40(3), pp. 866-892
- **DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206311423788

**Abstract summary**
The meta-analysis pools 34 studies on how hardline and softline bargaining strategies affect economic and socioemotional outcomes in distributive negotiations. It draws moderators from the graduated reciprocation in tension-reduction model and level of aspiration theory.

**Key findings**
- Hardline strategies produce higher economic outcomes, while softline strategies produce higher socioemotional outcomes.
- Hardline negotiators gain the most economically when visual contact is possible, when the opposing party is male, when they are instructed to maximize individual outcomes, and when they know the bargaining zone.
- Softline negotiators gain the most economically when they accurately reciprocate the opposing party's concessions.
- Contrary to predictions, softline bargaining does not prevail when the risk and cost of impasses are high.

**Effect sizes**
- Economic outcomes: 135 effect sizes
- Socioemotional outcomes: 30 effect sizes

The page reports only these counts. It does not give the magnitude of the effect sizes (e.g., d or r values) or confidence intervals, so you would need the full article to get those.

**Brooks & Schweitzer (2011), "Can Nervous Nelly Negotiate?"** The study is in *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes* (vol. 115, pp. 43–54). In four studies, the researchers induced either anxiety or neutral feelings and studied behavior in negotiation and continuous shrinking-pie tasks. Anxious negotiators set lower expectations, opened with lower offers, left talks sooner, and got worse final outcomes. The authors also found that negotiator self-efficacy moderates the relationship between anxiety and behavior; high self-efficacy mitigates the harmful effects of anxiety. A Harvard Business School summary describes the anxiety induction as playing the theme from the film *Psycho* before a mock cellphone-contract negotiation, and reports that anxious buyers ended up with a $6.60 final profit versus $7.94 for those who hadn't been exposed to incidental anxiety.

**Not covered:** Gunia, Swaab, Sivanathan & Galinsky (2013) on alternatives, and Morris, Larrick & Su (2009) on misperceiving negotiation counterparts, including the disclosing-reservation-price outcome. A follow-up search with the author names and journal titles, or with the paper titles alone, would be needed for those.

**Full abstract:** The page's full abstract is not reproduced here because it is copyrighted, but here is a summary. The authors test whether offering a choice among several equivalent first offers (Multiple Equivalent Simultaneous Offers, or MESOs) helps negotiators balance claiming and creating value. Across six experiments comparing MESOs to a single package offer, they report three effects:

1. **Stronger anchors and better outcomes for offerers**, because recipients saw MESOs as a more sincere attempt at agreement.
2. **Greater joint outcomes**, because MESOs were more likely to include an economically attractive starting point for recipients.
3. **A more cooperative reputation and negotiation climate** for the offerer.

The authors conclude that MESOs reduce the negotiator dilemma for both offerers and recipients.

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.007

**Authors:** Geoffrey J. Leonardelli, Jun Gu, Geordie McRuer, Victoria Husted Medvec, Adam D. Galinsky

**Journal:** *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes*, Volume 152, pp. 64–83, published 1 May 2019

**Study sample details:** The page reports only that the research involved six experiments comparing MESOs to a single package offer. It gives no participant numbers, demographics, recruitment methods, or per-experiment details. The supplementary materials and full article would be needed for those.

**Citation**
- **Authors:** Tey, K. S., Schaerer, M., Madan, N., & Swaab, R.
- **Year:** 2021
- **Title:** The Impact of Concession Patterns on Negotiations: When and Why Decreasing Concessions Lead to a Distributive Disadvantage
- **Journal:** *Organizational Behavior & Human Decision Processes*, vol. 165, pp. 153–166
- **DOI:** 10.1016/j.obhdp.2021.05.003

**Abstract summary**
- **Core idea:** A series of shrinking concessions (for example, $1,500, then $1,210, $1,180, $1,170) signals that a negotiator is nearing their limit. The authors argue this puts the offer recipient at a disadvantage.
- **Prevalence:** Most negotiators do not naturally use decreasing concessions.
- **Sample:** Seven studies with N = 2,311 participants in total. The page does not give per-study sample sizes.
- **Main findings:**
  - Recipients of decreasing concessions made less ambitious counteroffers (Studies 1–5).
  - Recipients reached worse deals (Study 2).
  - The mechanism is that decreasing concessions shape recipients' expectations about later offers. This inflates their estimate of the counterpart's reservation price (Study 3).
  - The penalty is largest when concessions decrease at a moderate rate (Study 4a) and when the decline spans more rounds (Study 4b).
  - Recipients can partly protect themselves by setting a target before negotiating (Study 5).

The paper you're looking for is in *Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin*, not *Psychological Science*. Its full title is "The remarkable robustness of the first-offer effect: Across culture, power, and issues." Gunia B. C., Swaab R. I., Sivanathan N., Galinsky A. D. (2013). The remarkable robustness of the first-offer effect: Across culture, power, and issues. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 39, 1547–1558.

**Findings:** The authors tested the effect across cultures, power levels, and single- versus multi-issue negotiations. Their first two studies found the effect holds across cultures and in multi-issue negotiations. Their last two found that low-power negotiators gain from moving first in both single- and multi-issue settings. First offers operate through the distributive issues, not the integrative or compatible issues. I didn't find the paper's full text, so the study details come only from the abstract.

**The BATNA finding is a different paper.** The Psychological Science research on weak BATNAs is by Schaerer, Swaab, and Galinsky, not Gunia et al. In it, negotiators with no BATNA were actually more successful than those with weak BATNAs, making higher initial offers that led to more profitable deals. If you're looking for that, search for the Schaerer, Swaab, and Galinsky Psychological Science paper on weak BATNAs.

The paper is **"Starting high and ending with nothing: The role of anchors and power in negotiations,"** published in the *Journal of Experimental Social Psychology* in 2012 (vol. 48, no. 1, pp. 226–231). Schweinsberg, M, Ku, G, Wang, C S and Pillutla, M are the listed authors, though the author order differs across databases.

The abstract's main findings, paraphrased:

- Prior research generally finds that making the first offer helps negotiators, but this paper tests whether extreme first offers backfire. It proposes that extreme first offers offend recipients and cause them to walk away, producing an impasse.
- Two experiments support this. Extreme offers carry risk: they can still anchor counteroffers and final outcomes in the offerer's favor, but only when an impasse is avoided (extreme offers can be risky).
- Power is a moderator. Low- and high-power negotiators are equally offended by extreme offers, but it is the low-power negotiators who walk away.

Two notes on sources. The Kellogg listing gives a different subtitle, "The disadvantages of high anchors in negotiations," which appears to be an alternate or working title. Also, the full text is not freely available from every repository; one institutional repository states full text not available from this repository, so the abstract is the part I could confirm.

Links: [{"title":"Anchoring: accessibility as a cause of judgmental assimilation","url":"https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/a/anchoring-accessibility-as-a-cause-of-judgmental-assimilation"},{"title":"Strack, Fritz, Bahnik, Stepan ORCID: 0000-0002-0579-6808 and Mussweiler, Thomas","url":"https://kups.ub.uni-koeln.de/25385/"},{"title":"atlantis-press.com","url":"https://www.atlantis-press.com/article/125983664.pdf"},{"title":"london.edu","url":"https://lbsresearch.london.edu/id/eprint/620"},{"title":"www.frontiersin.org","url":"https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01079/pdf"},{"title":"www.frontiersin.org","url":"https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00225/pdf"},{"title":"HarrisEtAl 2019 anchoring","url":"https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10074759/1/HarrisEtAl_2019_anchoring.pdf"},{"title":"journals.sagepub.com","url":"https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00332941211016750"},{"title":"anchoring and ahtml","url":"https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/anchoring-and-ahtml"}]

The search covered the selective accessibility model and the Furnham & Boo review, but not the "Many Analysts" or Klein Many Labs anchoring replications, so I couldn't confirm anything about those.

**Mussweiler & Strack (1999) and selective accessibility:** The original paper is "Hypothesis-consistent testing and semantic priming in the anchoring paradigm: A selective accessibility model," Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 35, 136–164. Later sources describe the model as proposing that anchoring is produced by enhanced accessibility of information consistent with the suggested anchor. A 2016 review by Strack, Bahnik and Mussweiler summarizes that anchoring is a result of selective accessibility of information compatible with an anchor.

**Furnham & Boo (2011):** Several papers cite this as a review of the anchoring literature. One paper notes that it reviews numerous experiments designed to validate and advance the anchoring effect. I didn't get the review's own abstract, so I can't say more about its contents.

**Replications:** A UCL study by Harris et al. (2019) is titled "Failures to replicate a key result of the selective accessibility theory of anchoring". This is relevant to the selective accessibility question, though I didn't retrieve its findings in detail. I found no results for a "Many Analysts" study or a Klein et al. Many Labs anchoring replication, so I can't confirm whether those exist or what they found. A follow-up search would be needed for those.

# Core experimental findings on bargaining behaviour (for an e-mail buyer agent with multi-issue term sheets)

Method note: web research only (about 15 search/fetch calls), no Tacto API. Everything below comes from search-result abstracts and publisher/repository pages. I read NO full texts. "Access" is my guess unless stated. Items marked [UNVERIFIED] came from my memory or a single secondary page and need a DOI check. Nearly all studies are lab or online experiments with students or panel participants, not field data.

## 1. First offers and anchoring

### Takeaway
The first-offer effect is large and robust in simple, single-issue, price-type bargaining, and it holds across power, culture and multi-issue settings. Its costs are impasse risk and lower benefit as complexity rises. Extreme offers anchor but can offend and cause walk-aways, especially from low-power recipients. Effect sizes come from one 2025 meta-analysis and are not final-paper verified.

### Cited Findings
- Meta-analysis of 90 studies (Petrowsky, Loschelder et al., OBHDP 2025, preregistered, robust variance estimation) plus experiments (Studies 2a-2b, N = 2,121). Making the first offer gives an advantage and ambitious first offers give economic gains, but ambitious offers raise impasse odds. Effects shrink as the number and type of issues increase, and the mechanisms change. Conference abstract values: first-mover g = 0.49, first-offer magnitude g = 1.30, offer-outcome r = 0.53 (pre-publication figures, check against the final paper). Heterogeneity is high. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104448. Access: the journal is paywalled, but a Leuphana PubData parallel publication (DOI 10.48548/pubdata-3207) appears open access. Abstract level only. — [Leuphana PubData](https://pubdata.leuphana.de/entities/publication/29dc7e5d-01eb-420a-b73d-66e0be7cd440); [FIS Leuphana summary](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/the-power-and-peril-of-first-offers-in-negotiations-a-conceptual-/)
- Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001), JPSP 81(4), 657-669. Three lab experiments: first offers anchor outcomes, and the effect is reduced when the counterpart takes perspective or focuses on their own target/BATNA information. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.657 [UNVERIFIED, from memory]. APA/library access (TUM). Abstract only. — [Kellogg record](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2001/first-offers-as-anchors-the-role-of-perspective-taking)
- Orr & Guthrie (2006), Ohio State J. on Dispute Resolution 21, 597; meta-analysis of simulated negotiations. Anchoring has a significant effect on deals, tested against experience and information environment. A secondary blog gives r about 0.50 (0.37 adjusted for experience); verify before use. Open access on bepress. Abstract only. — [bepress](https://works.bepress.com/chris-guthrie/18); [Vanderbilt IR](https://ir.vanderbilt.edu/handle/1803/7415); secondary: [Miles Mediation](https://milesmediation.com/blog/make-the-first-move-and-drop-the-anchor-miles-mediation/)
- Gunia, Swaab, Sivanathan & Galinsky (2013), PSPB 39, 1547-1558, "Remarkable robustness of the first-offer effect: across culture, power, and issues". The effect held across cultures and in multi-issue negotiations, and low-power negotiators gained from moving first. The first offer works through the distributive issues, not the integrative or compatible ones. DOI not retrieved. Abstract only. Lab. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/t/the-remarkable-robustness-of-the-first-offer-effect-across-culture-power-and-issues)
- Extreme offers: Schweinsberg, Ku, Wang & Pillutla (2012), JESP 48(1), 226-231, "Starting high and ending with nothing". Two experiments. Extreme first offers still anchor counteroffers and outcomes, but they offend recipients and risk impasse. Low-power and high-power recipients were equally offended, but low-power ones walked away. Abstract only. (A search note said the Kellogg subtitle differs; I did not check author order or the DOI.) — [LBS](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/s/starting-high-and-ending-with-nothing-the-role-of-anchors-and-power-in-negotiations); [ISB](https://eprints.exchange.isb.edu/id/eprint/1559/)
- Precision: Loschelder, Friese & Trötschel (2017), JESP 70, 164-176, three experiments. Precise anchors (e.g. 4,970 vs 5,000) anchor recipients more strongly, via an attribution of competence. Senders who use precise numbers choose less extreme (less ambitious) offers. Abstract level only; no effect sizes retrieved. — [Saarland repository](https://publikationen.sulb.uni-saarland.de/handle/20.500.11880/27829); [PON summary](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/negotiation-research-can-use-effective-first-offer-strive-precision-nb/?amp)
- Mussweiler & Strack (1999), JESP 35, 136-164, is the selective accessibility account of anchoring (anchor-consistent knowledge becomes more accessible). Harris et al. (2019) report failures to replicate a key result of that theory (UCL preprint; not read). I did not find a direct Many Labs anchoring replication via search; my memory says Many Labs 1 replicated classic anchoring, but this is unverified. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/a/anchoring-accessibility-as-a-cause-of-judgmental-assimilation); [UCL](https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10074759/1/HarrisEtAl_2019_anchoring.pdf)
- Brooks & Schweitzer (2011), OBHDP 115, 43-54: incidental anxiety lowered expectations and opening offers and worsened outcomes (four studies; HBS summary says $6.60 vs $7.94 in one study). Relevant only as evidence that low aspirations lower first offers. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v115y2011i1p43-54.html); [HBS](https://hbswk.hbs.edu/item/overcoming-nervous-nelly)

### Inferences
- For a buyer agent, anchor first with an ambitious but defensible opening, and keep it believable; reserve extreme offers for situations where walking away is not costly. This is an inference from Petrowsky, Schweinsberg and the Leonardelli entries below.
- With a precise (non-round) opening figure, the recipient may be anchored more strongly, but the agent should not shrink its ambition because of it. This is my inference from Loschelder et al.
- In a multi-issue term sheet the anchor effect is concentrated in the price (distributive) issue (Gunia 2013) and weakens as issues multiply (Petrowsky 2025).

### Gaps
- Final effect sizes, moderator tables and the exact impasse increase from Petrowsky 2025 were not read.
- No direct evidence on anchoring in e-mail or LLM-vs-LLM negotiation was found.
- Replication status of the negotiation-specific effects: no failed replication of the first-offer effect found; the replication of the cognitive mechanism is contested (Harris 2019).

## 2. Concession patterns

### Takeaway
Hard bargaining wins more money but costs relationship and, in some conditions, impasses. Reciprocating concessions is the best soft strategy. Shrinking concession steps signal a nearing limit and make recipients less ambitious; the evidence is a single 2021 lab paper plus older work.

### Cited Findings
- Hüffmeier, Freund, Zerres, Backhaus & Hertel (2014), J. Management 40(3), 866-892. Meta-analysis of 34 studies of distributive negotiation (135 economic and 30 socioemotional effect sizes). Hardline strategies gave higher economic outcomes and softline gave higher socioemotional outcomes. Hardliners gained most with visual contact, knowledge of the bargaining zone and a maximize-own-outcome instruction. Softliners did best when they accurately reciprocated concessions, and softline did not win even when impasse risk and cost were high (contrary to prediction). DOI 10.1177/0149206311423788. Likely paywalled (TUM). Abstract only; no d/r values retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/801197e8-e374-4128-aeb3-c66c06cb8812)
- Tey, Schaerer, Madan & Swaab (2021), OBHDP 165, 153-166. Seven studies, N = 2,311. Decreasing concession sequences (e.g. 1,500, 1,210, 1,180, 1,170) lead recipients to make less ambitious counteroffers and reach worse deals, mediated by an inflated estimate of the counterpart's reservation price. The effect is strongest for moderate decline rates and for declines over more rounds; setting a target in advance partly protects recipients. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2021.05.003. Abstract only. Lab/online. — [INSEAD](https://www.insead.edu/faculty-research/publications/journal-articles/impact-concession-patterns-negotiations-when-and-why)
- Lawler & MacMurray (1980), a programmed-opponent study cited in a search snippet: the best response depended on the opponent's opening stance, and prior deadlock reduced concessions. Single secondary snippet, not verified. — [Leuphana snippet](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/concession-patterns-in-dyadic-negotiations-empirically-contrastin/)
- A separate study (found via the same search, authors not retrieved) reports that distributive concession making raises impasse rates, driven by loss of conceded value and not by reciprocity-norm violation. — [TU Dortmund](https://eldorado.tu-dortmund.de/items/f909800c-1d5e-4cb0-9fa9-9745ab154670/full)

### Inferences
- A seller-facing buyer agent should avoid showing a clear shrinking-step pattern if it wants to hide its limit, and should expect a seller using one to be signalling a limit (but it may be a bluff).
- Reciprocate counterpart concessions in kind; start tough and concede on a pattern that does not leak the limit.

### Gaps
- No meta-analysis on concession timing found; no evidence tied specifically to e-mail asynchronous bargaining.
- Effect sizes of Hüffmeier 2014 not retrieved.

## 3. BATNA, reservation prices and power

### Takeaway
Better alternatives raise outcomes and the propensity to move first, but the first-offer anchor can outweigh BATNA effects and, per one study, having no BATNA can beat a weak one. Evidence on disclosing information is weak in my findings.

### Cited Findings
- Kim & Fragale (2005), J. Applied Psychology 90(2), 373-381. BATNA advantage mattered more when the bargaining zone was small, contribution advantage when it was large. DOI 10.1037/0021-9010.90.2.373 (as found by search; not opened). Abstract level. — [summary page](https://academicnewsletter.sufe.edu.cn/info/372348)
- Magee, Galinsky & Gruenfeld (2007), PSPB 33(2), 200-212. Five experiments. Higher power increased propensity to negotiate and to move first; negotiators with strong BATNAs were over three times as likely to intend to open (as reported by the abstract summary); making the first offer gave a bargaining edge. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/2007/power-propensity-to-negotiate-and-moving-first-in-competitive/?p=1)
- Pinkley, Neale & Bennett (1994), OBHDP 57(1), 97-116, "The impact of alternatives to settlement in dyadic negotiation". Content not retrieved; only the citation. A 1995 Pinkley OBHDP paper on BATNA knowledge was not confirmed. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v57y1994i1p97-116.html)
- Schaerer, Swaab & Galinsky, Psychological Science (about 2015; year and title unconfirmed): negotiators with no BATNA did better than those with weak BATNAs, because they made higher first offers (anchors weigh more than power). Seen only in a search note; [UNVERIFIED]. — [APS](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/minds-business/negotiating-with-nothing-holds-surprise-benefits.html)
- Schweinsberg et al. 2012 (section 1): power moderates whether extreme anchors lead to walk-aways.
- Gunia, Brett, Nandkeolyar & Kamdar (2011), J. Applied Psychology 96(4), 774-789, three studies: lower interpersonal trust in Indian negotiators went with less information-sharing and lower joint gains than for US negotiators. Relevant to information exchange, not BATNA. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2011/paying-a-price-culture-trust-and-negotiation-consequences/?p=1)
- Kong, Dirks & Ferrin (2014), Acad. Management J. 57(5), 1235-1255. Meta-analysis of 38 independent studies on trust within negotiations, with three contingencies. Effect sizes not retrieved. — [MetaTOC](https://metatoc.com/papers/23303-interpersonal-trust-within-negotiations-meta-analytic-evidence-critical-contingencies-and-directions-for-future-research)

### Inferences
- A buyer agent should have its BATNA/reservation value internally and may move first when its BATNA is good, but should not reveal the reservation price (no direct evidence retrieved on disclosure; this is a design judgment). Evidence is largely lab.

### Gaps
- Evidence on disclosing versus hiding BATNA/reservation price (Pinkley 1995, Morris/Larrick/Su, Gunia et al. alternatives) was not retrieved. Treat as open.
- Replication status of the weak-BATNA result is unknown.

## 4. Multi-issue offers, MESOs, logrolling, questions, information

### Takeaway
MESOs, information exchange and question-asking raise joint gains and rapport in lab studies; the fixed-pie bias is the main obstacle. A buyer agent sending packages with several equivalent options should gain both anchoring and integrative benefits. The evidence is lab-based.

### Cited Findings
- Leonardelli, Gu, McRuer, Medvec & Galinsky (2019), OBHDP 152, 64-83, six experiments. MESOs (multiple equivalent simultaneous offers) vs a single package: stronger anchors and better outcomes for the offerer (recipients saw them as more sincere), greater joint outcomes, and a more cooperative climate. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.007. Abstract only; participant numbers not retrieved. — [Macquarie](https://researchers.mq.edu.au/en/publications/multiple-equivalent-simultaneous-offers-mesos-reduce-the-negotiat/)
- Thompson (1991), JESP 27(2)? (a search result said 40(2), 161-179; volume/pages inconsistent, check) "Information exchange in negotiation". Giving and seeking information both improved accuracy of judgment and produced more integrative agreements, even when only one side did so. Abstract only. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1991/information-exchange-in-negotiation)
- Thompson & Hastie (1990), Org. Behav. Human Decis. Processes, "Judgment tasks and biases in negotiation" (my memory for the title; the page said "Social perception in negotiation"-type content; check): fixed-sum assumption is widespread; people who missed integrative potential got lower individual and joint profit; many learn through negotiation. Abstract level. — [Kellogg](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/academics-research/research/detail/1990/judgment-tasks-and-biases-in-negotiation/)
- Bazerman & Neale (1983) is the origin of the biases framework (secondary source only). A 2002 JBDM study on initial perceptions found logrolling offers were not judged more attractive, did not dispel the fixed-pie assumption, but still gave the initiator and the pair higher profit. — [CRIS HUJI](https://cris.huji.ac.il/en/publications/initial-perceptions-in-negotiations-evaluation-and-response-to-lo-2/)
- Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017), JPSP 113(3), 430-452. Question-asking, especially follow-up questions, increased liking via perceived responsiveness; people do not predict this. This is about liking in conversation (including speed dating), not negotiation outcomes. DOI 10.1037/pspi0000097. Open author copy at Harvard DASH. Abstract only. — [DASH](https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/73120379-2eb6-6bd4-e053-0100007fdf3b)
- De Dreu, Weingart & Kwon (2000), JPSP 78, 889-905. Meta-analysis of 28 studies: prosocial negotiators were less contentious, solved problems more and got higher joint outcomes, but only when resistance to yielding was high or unknown. No effect size retrieved. — [UvA DARE](https://dare.uva.nl/id/403ebedc-c455-47a0-8a00-803afaed87b3)
- Thompson, Wang & Gunia (2010), Annual Review of Psychology 61, 491-515, "Negotiation": review at five levels (intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, organizational, virtual) on value creation and claiming. # Core experimental findings on bargaining behaviour (for an e-mail buyer agent with multi-issue term sheets)

Method note: web research only (about 15 search/fetch calls), no Tacto API. Everything below comes from search-result abstracts and publisher/repository pages. I read NO full texts. "Access" is my guess unless stated. Items marked [UNVERIFIED] came from my memory or a single secondary page and need a DOI check. Nearly all studies are lab or online experiments with students or panel participants, not field data.

## 1. First offers and anchoring

### Takeaway
The first-offer effect is large and robust in simple, single-issue, price-type bargaining, and it holds across power, culture and multi-issue settings. Its costs are impasse risk and lower benefit as complexity rises. Extreme offers anchor but can offend and cause walk-aways, especially from low-power recipients. Effect sizes come from one 2025 meta-analysis and are not final-paper verified.

### Cited Findings
- Meta-analysis of 90 studies (Petrowsky, Loschelder et al., OBHDP 2025, preregistered, robust variance estimation) plus experiments (Studies 2a-2b, N = 2,121). Making the first offer gives an advantage and ambitious first offers give economic gains, but ambitious offers raise impasse odds. Effects shrink as the number and type of issues increase, and the mechanisms change. Conference abstract values: first-mover g = 0.49, first-offer magnitude g = 1.30, offer-outcome r = 0.53 (pre-publication figures, check against the final paper). Heterogeneity is high. DOI 10.1016/j.obhdp.2025.104448. Access: the journal is paywalled, but a Leuphana PubData parallel publication (DOI 10.48548/pubdata-3207) appears open access. Abstract level only. — [Leuphana PubData](https://pubdata.leuphana.de/entities/publication/29dc7e5d-01eb-420a-b73d-66e0be7cd440); [FIS Leuphana summary](https://fis.leuphana.de/en/publications/the-power-and-peril-of-first-offers-in-negotiations-a-conceptual-/)
- Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001), JPSP 81(4), 657-669. Three lab experiments: first offers anchor outcomes, and the effect is reduced when the counterpart takes perspective or focuses on their own target/BATNA information. DOI 10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.657 [UNVERIFIED, from memory]. APA/library access (TUM). Abstract only. — [Kellogg record](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/2001/first-offers-as-anchors-the-role-of-perspective-taking)
- Orr & Guthrie (2006), Ohio State J. on Dispute Resolution 21, 597; meta-analysis of simulated negotiations. Anchoring has a significant effect on deals, tested against experience and information environment. A secondary blog gives r about 0.50 (0.37 adjusted for experience); verify before use. Open access on bepress. Abstract only. — [bepress](https://works.bepress.com/chris-guthrie/18); [Vanderbilt IR](https://ir.vanderbilt.edu/handle/1803/7415); secondary: [Miles Mediation](https://milesmediation.com/blog/make-the-first-move-and-drop-the-anchor-miles-mediation/)
- Gunia, Swaab, Sivanathan & Galinsky (2013), PSPB 39, 1547-1558, "Remarkable robustness of the first-offer effect: across culture, power, and issues". The effect held across cultures and in multi-issue negotiations, and low-power negotiators gained from moving first. The first offer works through the distributive issues, not the integrative or compatible ones. DOI not retrieved. Abstract only. Lab. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/t/the-remarkable-robustness-of-the-first-offer-effect-across-culture-power-and-issues)
- Extreme offers: Schweinsberg, Ku, Wang & Pillutla (2012), JESP 48(1), 226-231, "Starting high and ending with nothing". Two experiments. Extreme first offers still anchor counteroffers and outcomes, but they offend recipients and risk impasse. Low-power and high-power recipients were equally offended, but low-power ones walked away. Abstract only. (A search note said the Kellogg subtitle differs; I did not check author order or the DOI.) — [LBS](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/s/starting-high-and-ending-with-nothing-the-role-of-anchors-and-power-in-negotiations); [ISB](https://eprints.exchange.isb.edu/id/eprint/1559/)
- Precision: Loschelder, Friese & Trötschel (2017), JESP 70, 164-176, three experiments. Precise anchors (e.g. 4,970 vs 5,000) anchor recipients more strongly, via an attribution of competence. Senders who use precise numbers choose less extreme (less ambitious) offers. Abstract level only; no effect sizes retrieved. — [Saarland repository](https://publikationen.sulb.uni-saarland.de/handle/20.500.11880/27829); [PON summary](https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/dealmaking-daily/negotiation-research-can-use-effective-first-offer-strive-precision-nb/?amp)
- Mussweiler & Strack (1999), JESP 35, 136-164, is the selective accessibility account of anchoring (anchor-consistent knowledge becomes more accessible). Harris et al. (2019) report failures to replicate a key result of that theory (UCL preprint; not read). I did not find a direct Many Labs anchoring replication via search; my memory says Many Labs 1 replicated classic anchoring, but this is unverified. — [LBS record](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/a/anchoring-accessibility-as-a-cause-of-judgmental-assimilation); [UCL](https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10074759/1/HarrisEtAl_2019_anchoring.pdf)
- Brooks & Schweitzer (2011), OBHDP 115, 43-54: incidental anxiety lowered expectations and opening offers and worsened outcomes (four studies; HBS summary says $6.60 vs $7.94 in one study). Relevant only as evidence that low aspirations lower first offers. — [IDEAS](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v115y2011i1p43-54.html); [HBS](https://hbswk.hbs.edu/item/overcoming-nervous-nelly)
